params.question: According to the WHO xerophthalmia staging, up to which stage can vitamin A deficiency be managed at a primary health centre without specialist referral?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Night blindness (XN) does respond to vitamin A supplementation at a PHC, but management there is not limited to this earliest stage — stages up to and including X1B can be managed without specialist referral.

Correct. Stages XN through X1B — including conjunctival xerosis (X1A) — respond well to high-dose vitamin A at a primary health centre. Stage X2 (corneal xerosis) and beyond require urgent specialist referral, as corneal involvement risks permanent blindness.
Stage X2 marks the onset of corneal involvement and is the critical referral threshold. At this stage, specialist care is urgent — primary health centre management is sufficient only up to stage X1B.

answers.text: X3A (keratomalacia involving less than one-third of the cornea)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Keratomalacia (X3A) represents advanced corneal disease with risk of perforation within hours. This demands specialist intervention well beyond primary care capabilities. The referral threshold begins earlier, at stage X2.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the WHO staging order: XN → X1A → X1B → X2 → X3A → X3B → XS → XF. The cornea is the line — stages through X1B (conjunctival) respond to vitamin A at a PHC; X2 (corneal xerosis) and beyond need urgent specialist referral.
Well done. The cornea is the dividing line: conjunctival stages (up to X1B) are managed at the PHC, while any corneal involvement (X2 onward) demands urgent specialist referral.

interactions.label: Acid burns to the eye are more destructive than alkali burns because acid penetr

params.question: Acid burns to the eye are more destructive than alkali burns because acid penetrates deeper into the ocular tissues.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: The statement is false. Alkali burns are more destructive, not acid. Acid causes coagulative necrosis — denatured surface proteins form a barrier that limits penetration. Alkali causes liquefactive necrosis, dissolving tissues continuously with no barrier, allowing it to penetrate through the cornea into the anterior chamber minute by minute.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — the statement is false. Alkali burns are more destructive. Acid causes coagulative necrosis, denaturing surface proteins into a barrier that limits penetration depth. Alkali causes liquefactive necrosis, dissolving cell membranes continuously without forming any barrier, and penetrates through the cornea into the anterior chamber.

interactions.label: A patient presents with a blind, painful eye. B-scan ultrasonography confirms no

params.question: A patient presents with a blind, painful eye. B-scan ultrasonography confirms no intraocular mass. Which procedure is indicated?

answers.text: Enucleation, because the entire globe must be removed to prevent sympathetic ophthalmia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Enucleation is reserved for when a tumour is present or suspected, or when sympathetic ophthalmia must be prevented after a penetrating injury (within 10–14 days). This patient has a confirmed tumour-free eye with no history of penetrating injury — the less radical evisceration is preferred.

answers.text: Evisceration, because the scleral shell and extraocular muscles are preserved for superior cosmesis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The decision algorithm: tumour present → enucleate; no tumour, blind painful eye → eviscerate; orbital spread → exenterate. B-scan has excluded a hidden mass. Evisceration removes the intraocular contents while preserving the scleral shell and attached muscles, giving the best socket motility and cosmetic outcome.

answers.text: Exenteration, because complete orbital clearance is needed to eliminate the source of pain

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Exenteration removes the entire orbital contents — globe, muscles, fat, lacrimal gland, and often the eyelids. It is reserved for orbital malignancies with extraocular spread or rhino-orbital mucormycosis — far more radical than needed for a blind painful eye without orbital disease.

answers.text: Enucleation, because evisceration risks leaving malignant cells behind in the scleral shell

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This concern applies only when a tumour is present or suspected — the sclera's emissary canals can allow tumour spread. Here, B-scan has confirmed no intraocular mass, so evisceration is safe and preferred. The B-scan is the critical safeguard — never perform evisceration without it.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the algorithm: tumour → enucleate, no tumour → eviscerate, orbital spread → exenterate. A B-scan must always precede evisceration to exclude a hidden intraocular mass.
Exactly right. The B-scan is the critical safeguard — it excludes a hidden melanoma before committing to evisceration. A blind painful eye can conceal a tumour, and the B-scan is not optional.

interactions.label: Approximately 80 per cent of global blindness is classified as 'avoidable.' Whic

params.question: Approximately 80 per cent of global blindness is classified as 'avoidable.' Which of the following best explains this classification?

answers.text: Most causes of blindness are genetic conditions detectable through screening programmes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The vast majority of avoidable blindness is caused by acquired conditions — cataract, refractive error, vitamin A deficiency, and trachoma. Screening helps detect these, but the conditions themselves are not genetic in origin.

answers.text: The majority of causes are either preventable through public health measures or treatable with existing surgical and optical interventions

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. 'Avoidable blindness' encompasses two categories: preventable causes (vitamin A deficiency, trachoma) addressed by public health measures, and treatable causes (cataract, refractive error) addressed by surgery or spectacles. In India, cataract alone accounts for about two-thirds of bilateral blindness.

answers.text: Modern laser technology can reverse visual loss in most forms of blindness

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Laser surgery treats some conditions, but the avoidable blindness burden is driven by cataract (needing IOL surgery), refractive error (needing spectacles), and preventable nutritional and infectious causes — conditions addressed by simpler, more widely deployable interventions.

answers.text: Blindness rates decline automatically as countries develop economically

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Economic development supports healthcare infrastructure, but blindness does not decline without targeted intervention. Programmes like NPCBVI and Vision 2020 exist because barriers — fear, transport costs, lack of escorts, delayed presentation — persist even when free surgery is available.

overallFeedback.feedback: Avoidable blindness = preventable (vitamin A deficiency, trachoma) + treatable (cataract, refractive error). About 80% of global blindness falls into one of these categories, which is why programmes like NPCBVI and Vision 2020 focus on both public health prevention and accessible treatment.
Well answered. The preventable-versus-treatable framework is central to community ophthalmology and shapes every national blindness control programme, including India's NPCBVI.
